TITLE / ONE-LINER

If an investor reads only this slide, they should know what you do. Use a plain-language one-liner (YC style: 'We help [who] do [what]'), not a slogan. Avoid jargon and buzzwords.

The raise chip is optional; some founders prefer to save the ask for the end. In a cold, send-ahead deck it's useful up front.

PROBLEM (Sequoia: 'Describe the pain of the customer'; YC: 'Why is this a big, urgent problem?')

- Who has the problem, specifically? Name the customer segment.
- How painful is it? Quantify in time, money, or risk.
- How do they solve it today, and why does that fall short?
- One sharp stat or a short customer quote is more persuasive than a list.

Investors need to believe the problem is real, frequent, and expensive before they care about your solution.

SOLUTION (Sequoia: 'Demonstrate your company's value proposition')

- Focus on what changes for the customer, not on a feature list.
- Make the before/after contrast obvious and, if possible, measurable.
- The 'insight' line is your secret: what you know that incumbents and other founders don't. Strong insights are often counter-intuitive.

PRODUCT / DEMO

- Show, don't tell: real screenshots beat mockups; a short GIF or live demo beats both.
- Call out the 'magic moment', the point where the user gets value.
- Mention the product roadmap only briefly; you can put it in the appendix.
- If you're pre-product, show the prototype and what you've validated with users.

WHY NOW (Sequoia: 'Set up the historical evolution of your category. Why hasn't this been done before?')

- Investors look hard at this slide: great ideas often failed because they were too early.
- Common 'why now' drivers: a new platform or technology (e.g., AI models, cheaper sensors), a regulatory change, a behavior shift, a collapse in cost, or a market dislocation.
- You don't need all three cards; one compelling shift is better than three weak ones.

MARKET SIZE (Sequoia: 'Identify/profile the customer you cater to')

- Build the number bottom-up: (number of target customers) × (what each pays per year). Top-down figures ('1% of a $50B market') are a red flag to most VCs.
- Venture investors generally need to see a path to a $1B+ company, so the TAM should support that.
- Show your math, or keep it ready for the appendix; cite sources for any third-party numbers.

BUSINESS MODEL (Sequoia: 'Revenue model, pricing, average account size, lifetime value')

- Who pays, how much, how often? (subscription, usage-based, transaction fee, marketplace take rate…)
- Swap the pricing tiers for a single price if that's simpler; delete what you don't need.
- Unit economics: only show what you actually have. At pre-seed it's fine to show target or early numbers, labeled as such.
- Rough benchmarks investors use for SaaS: LTV:CAC ≥ 3:1, CAC payback < 12–18 months, gross margin 70%+.

TRACTION (YC: 'This is often the most important slide')

- Put your single best number in the headline and make it big.
- Show growth over time, not a snapshot: a chart going up and to the right is the point of this slide.
- The chart uses SAMPLE data. Right-click it → Edit Data to enter your real numbers.
- Pick metrics that fit your stage: revenue/MRR, active users, retention, paid pilots, LOIs, waitlist, notable customer logos.
- If traction is your strongest card, move this slide up to right after the Solution.

COMPETITION (Sequoia: 'List competitors; list your plan to win')

- Never say 'we have no competitors'. It signals naïveté or no market. Include the status quo (spreadsheets, doing nothing) and big incumbents.
- Pick 2×2 axes that genuinely matter to customers and honestly put you in the top-right. If the axes feel contrived, use a comparison table instead.
- The 'why we win' column matters more than the chart: what's defensible and gets stronger over time?

GO-TO-MARKET

- How do you find, win, and keep customers, and how does that scale?
- Be specific about the first channel that works; 'viral growth' or 'partnerships' with no evidence won't land.
- If you have data (CAC by channel, conversion rates, sales cycle length, pipeline), it belongs here.

TEAM (Sequoia: 'Founders, management, board of directors/advisors')

- At early stages, investors are betting on the team more than anything else.
- For each person, give the one credential that makes them uniquely suited to THIS problem (domain expertise, prior startup or exit, technical depth), not a full CV.
- Show how long the founders have worked together and that you're full-time.
- Delete or add cards to match your team; notable advisors and angels go in the bottom line.

FINANCIALS

- Keep it high level: 3–5 years of revenue, burn, and headcount. Detailed models go in the appendix or data room.
- Investors know projections are guesses; they're judging whether your assumptions are reasonable and whether you understand your business's drivers.
- Pre-revenue? Show the plan for the next 18–24 months and the milestones that unlock the next round instead.
- Rename the year columns (e.g., 2027, 2028…) and delete rows you don't need.

THE ASK / USE OF FUNDS

- State the amount, instrument (SAFE or priced round), and anything already committed or a lead investor.
- Tie the money to milestones: 'this round gets us to X, which sets us up for the next round'. Investors fund milestones, not runway.
- 18–24 months of runway is a typical target.
- The doughnut uses a placeholder 25/25/25/25 split. Right-click → Edit Data to change it.

VISION / CLOSE

- End on the big picture: if everything works, what does this company become in 10 years?
- Leave contact details on screen during Q&A.
- Optionally restate the ask in one line.

APPENDIX

Backup slides for diligence questions. Keep them out of the main flow, but have them ready. Typical contents: detailed model, cohort/retention curves, customer references and case studies, technical deep-dive, roadmap, cap table, and full TAM math.

Duplicate any content slide (right-click → Duplicate Slide) to build these.
